tagline: Forests, marshes, and ten thousand lakes
overview:
Belarus is a landlocked country in Eastern Europe, wedged between Poland, Lithuania, Latvia, Russia, and Ukraine. At about 207,600 square kilometers it is close to the size of Kansas, and much like Kansas it is flat, but here the plains are covered by dense forests, slow rivers, and thousands of lakes rather than wheat. Around 9 million people live in Belarus, and about two million of them are in the capital, Minsk, a city of wide avenues and grand Soviet-era buildings rebuilt after World War II.

Belarusian and Russian are both official languages, and Russian is what most people use day to day. Belarus was part of the Soviet Union until 1991. It is a republic with a president who has held office since 1994; elections have been widely disputed, and huge protests followed the 2020 vote. The country keeps close ties with Russia. Belarusians are known for tractors and trucks built in Minsk, a growing software industry, and a deep love of potatoes, which appear in hundreds of dishes.
landAndNature: Glaciers flattened Belarus long ago, leaving gentle hills, sandy soils, and about 11,000 lakes. The highest point, Dzyarzhynskaya Hara, is only 345 meters. In the south spread the Pripyat Marshes, one of the largest wetlands in Europe, where rivers overflow each spring into a watery world of reeds, storks, and rare birds. Forests cover roughly 40 percent of the country. Belavezhskaya Pushcha, an ancient forest shared with Poland, protects the largest herd of European bison, the continent's heaviest land animal, along with wolves, lynx, and moose. Major rivers include the Dnieper and the Neman. The 1986 Chernobyl nuclear disaster in neighboring Ukraine dropped much of its radioactive fallout on southern Belarus, and part of that region remains a closed reserve.
peopleAndCulture: Most Belarusians are Orthodox Christians, with a Catholic minority in the west. Potatoes are the heart of the kitchen: draniki are crisp potato pancakes eaten with sour cream, and there are said to be hundreds of other potato recipes, along with borscht, mushroom soups, and kvass, a fizzy drink made from bread. Traditional shirts embroidered in red geometric patterns are worn at festivals like Kupalle, the midsummer night when people jump over bonfires and float flower wreaths on rivers. Straw weaving and the Slutsk sash, a richly patterned silk belt, are national crafts. Ice hockey and biathlon are the most followed sports. The painter Marc Chagall was born in Vitebsk, and writer Svetlana Alexievich won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2015.
history: Slavic tribes settled these forests over a thousand years ago and founded the Principality of Polotsk. In the 1200s and 1300s the Belarusian lands became the core of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, which later joined with Poland in a vast commonwealth. At the end of the 1700s the Russian Empire absorbed the region. After a brief independent republic in 1918, Belarus became a Soviet republic. World War II was catastrophic: roughly a quarter of the population died, Minsk was almost totally destroyed, and nearly all of the country's large Jewish community was murdered in the Holocaust. Belarus declared independence in 1991 as the Soviet Union broke apart. Alexander Lukashenko became president in 1994 and has stayed in power since, and the 2020 protests were met with mass arrests.
funFacts: The National Library of Belarus in Minsk is shaped like a giant glass diamond with 24 sides and lights up in colors at night.
Belarus, then a Soviet republic, was a founding member of the United Nations in 1945, even though it was not independent.
The country is sometimes called the lungs of Europe because of its huge forests and marshes.
Belarus tractors have been sold to more than 100 countries, and a model is even displayed in a Minsk museum.
The Mir and Nesvizh castles, both UNESCO World Heritage Sites, look like fairy-tale fortresses with red brick towers.
